flawed_step: Step 1: Identical degree sequences justify pairing vertices by degree. Step 2 would need to infer that such a pairing preserves adjacency, but degree data do not determine which vertices are adjacent. This step is unjustified.
counterexample: Let T1 have vertices {a,b,c,x,y,z} and edges {(a,b),(b,c),(a,x),(a,y),(c,z)}. Let T2 have the same vertex set and edges {(a,b),(b,c),(b,x),(a,y),(c,z)}. Each graph is simple and connected and has 6 vertices and 5 edges, hence is a tree. Both degree sequences are (3,2,2,1,1,1). In T1, the unique degree-3 vertex a has two degree-1 neighbors, x and y. In T2, the unique degree-3 vertex b has only one degree-1 neighbor, x. An isomorphism must map the unique degree-3 vertex to the unique degree-3 vertex and preserve the degrees of its neighbors, so no isomorphism exists.
assessment_summary: The proof attempt fails when equality of degree sequences must be promoted to an edge-preserving bijection. The explicit pair of trees above has identical degree sequences but is distinguished by the number of leaf neighbors of its unique degree-3 vertex.
